questions.problem:
Complete the following parametric equations generating the hyperbola $2{x}^{2}-8{y}^{2}=16$ in terms of the parameter $t,$ defined for $t\in [-\pi ,\pi ]$ where $t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.$

$x=2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,$
$y=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

First, we rewrite the equation of our hyperbola in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-8{y}^{2} & =16 \\ \frac{2{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{8{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our case, we have $a=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$ and $b=\sqrt{2}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x=2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm 4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(\pm a,0).$ From the graph, we have that $(1,0)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=1.$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y=\pm 4x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{4}{1} \\ \frac{b}{1} & =\frac{4}{1} \\ b & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{5}} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{5} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given Algebraically
canonical_examples.problem: What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola $\displaystyle\frac{x^2}{49} - \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\sec{t},\quad y=b\tan{t}.
$$

In our case, $a = \sqrt{49} = 7$ and $b =\sqrt9= 3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x=7\sec{t},\quad y=3\tan{t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given Graphically
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the asymptotes of the hyperbola below are $y=\pm\dfrac{5}{7}x,$ find the parametric equations of the hyperbola.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14077122/assets/fd2618e961c15a9b0665e73e18544ab08b0d611b962bc3771558c61450cf49e5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\sec{t},\quad y=b\tan{t},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(\pm a, 0).$ From the graph, we have that $(7,0)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=7.$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola are $y=\pm \dfrac{b}{a}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y=\pm\dfrac57x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{5}{7} \\ \frac{b}{7} & =\frac{5}{7} \\ b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=7\sec{t},\quad y=5\tan{t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola with the parametric equations $x = 6\sec{t},\, y = 4 \sqrt{2}\tan{t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\sec t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{6} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ {(\frac{x}{6})}^{2} & ={(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\tan{t}$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{4\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {(\frac{y}{4\sqrt{2}})}^{2} & ={(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{(4\sqrt{2})}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{32} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity $\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{32}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{32} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
